facts.value: £129.9m at 31 December 2025 — all PWLB, weighted 3.55%. Committed external borrowing forecast to run off to £115.8m (31/3/26), £109.2m (31/3/27), £102.6m (31/3/28), £96.0m (31/3/29) before any refinancing decision. No other long-term liabilities beyond £2.9m of leases which sit inside the Loans CFR line

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Para 1.12 states £129.9m borrowing/£47.1m investments at 31/12/25. Appendix B PWLB-only table prints the 3.55% weighted rate on the £129.9m. Table 2 (Appendix 1 section 3) shows the committed run-off through 31/3/29. Authorised limit £236.7m (para 1.24); operational boundary £213.9m; Q3 25/26 actual maximum £134.9m against 2024/25 limits (Appendix C).

facts.value: Total CFR £164.6m at 31 March 2025 actual, rising to £214.9m at 31 March 2029 forecast. GF CFR £27.3m → £33.5m (flat); HRA CFR £27.4m → £87.8m (3.2x, driven by Housing Development Programme, Housing Energy Improvements and Planned Maintenance); HRA Settlement debt £109.9m → £93.5m (running down). Loans CFR (Total CFR + leases £2.9m) £167.4m → £217.7m

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Table 2 (Appendix 1 section 3). Para 1.14 attributes the GF CFR rise to 'the new Waste Strategy' and notes 'New commercial and residential investment schemes have currently been put on hold due to the current interest rates making schemes less viable'. HRA CFR increase attributed to 'requirements arising from Housing Energy Improvements, Planned Maintenance and the current Housing Development Programme'. The Table 2 arithmetic is 'Total CFR + leases 2.9' = Loans CFR — the leases sit inside Loans CFR here, not outside. Balance-sheet identity below uses Loans CFR.

facts.value: £34.5m at 31 March 2025 actual, rising to £121.7m at 31 March 2029 forecast — a £87.2m expansion over four years. Balance sheet resources drop from £66.9m to £35.6m over the same period (down £31.3m); committed external borrowing runs off from £132.9m to £96.0m (down £36.9m). Combined, about £68m of new gap opens between resources and Loans CFR

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Table 2 (Appendix 1 section 3). Para 1.19 states plainly for the opening year: 'the difference of £34.5m between the CFR and external borrowing is internal borrowing which is where the Council has used its own resources to fund its borrowing requirement'. Para 1.14 flags 'the Council will be internally borrowed beyond the resources available for investment. At this point, an external borrowing position sets in'. Para 1.22 confirms: 'external borrowing the Council has already arranged will not be sufficient... additional borrowing may be required'.

facts.value: £110.5m at 31/03/25 actual, rising to £137.3m (26), £157.7m (27), £176.1m (28) and peaking at £192.1m at 31/03/29. Appendix D 50-year projection shows peak 2029 then steady decline; liability benchmark crosses zero around 2052; fixed-rate loans line drops from ~£130m in 2025 to ~£10m by 2053

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Table 3 (Appendix 1 section 3) and Graph 1/Appendix D. LB identity closes exactly for all five years: Loans CFR − Balance sheet resources + £10m liquidity allowance = LB. Para 1.20 rightly cautions that the 50-year graph assumes 'no new capital projects will begin after 2028/29, which is a very unlikely scenario' — do not lead externally on a 25y+ projection.

facts.value: 5% of PWLB fixed-rate book inside 12 months (against 25% upper limit); 5% in the following year; 13% in 24 months-5 years; 16% in 5-10 years; 61% at 10 years and above. On £129.9m PWLB at 31/12/25, 10% inside two years is c£13m; 61% at 10+ years is c£79m

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Appendix C refinancing rate risk indicator at 31/12/25. Distinctly long book compared with the sector we have read — Medway £245m inside two years, Redbridge £108.5m inside two, Northumberland £121m inside two, Shropshire 30% inside two. New Forest sits at the safe end of the distribution.

facts.value: £47.1m investments variable (all treated as variable because all short-term investments roll within 12 months — Appendix 1 Table 6); £2.5m borrowing variable. +/- 1% rate change = +/- £0.5m on investments, +/- £0.0m on borrowing (rounded)

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Table 6 (Appendix 1 section 6). Borrowing side is essentially all fixed-rate PWLB, so the only rate exposure is on the investment side. This is another feature of a defensively-built book — they carry the reinvestment risk not the refinancing risk.

facts.value: Not printed as a standalone indicator in this paper. Debt interest 2026/27 budget £5.7m; investment income £1.7m; implied net revenue cost £4.0m. Financial implications paragraph gives the average portfolio at £150.8m and average interest rate 3.77% (para 1.83)

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Para 1.83. The £150.8m average portfolio sits between year-open external of £115.8m (31/3/26 fc) and year-close £109.2m (31/3/27 fc) on the committed profile, so the £150.8m figure anticipates significant in-year new borrowing — consistent with paras 1.24, 1.28 and 1.29 (forward-starting loans in 2026/27 explicitly flagged). New Forest is a district and does not print the FCS/NRS ratio directly; total funding is not visible from this paper alone.

facts.value: Internal + short-term preference. Para 1.26: 'Short-term interest rates are currently higher than in the recent past but are expected to fall in the coming year and it is therefore likely to be more cost effective over the medium term to either use internal resources, or borrow short-term loans instead.' Forward-starting loans in 2026/27 explicitly flagged (para 1.29). Diversification of sources beyond PWLB (para 1.28) — banks, pensions, other local authorities, bonds. Hampshire Pension Fund explicitly excluded

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Paras 1.26–1.30. Arlingclose central case at Appendix A took Bank Rate to 3.25% by Q2 2026. On the 14 August 2026 PM fixing Bank Rate is still 3.75% — no cut in six months. PWLB Certainty rates at the long end have drifted higher rather than lower against the December central case: today 20y at 6.38%, 50y at 6.27%; the December central case for the 20y gilt was 5.13% (implying c5.93% Certainty). The short/long spread the strategy leans on has not narrowed — the value of the internal-and-short-term stance has held up better than the paper's own arithmetic implied.

facts.value: £9.1m at 31 December 2025 across pooled property (£7.6m at 4.46% income return) and pooled equity (£1.5m at 7.60%). Unrealised capital loss of £0.336m as at strategy date; Treasury Management Reserve balance £0.300m. Gap of £0.036m. Statutory IFRS 9 override extended to 31 March 2028 for investments made before 1 April 2024

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report — Council 26 February 2026

facts.note: Paras 1.44–1.45. Small numerical gap (£36k) but a dated one — three financial years for the loss to recover before it hits the CIES. Sector-wide theme; several councils' TMSSs describe similar override cliffs (see Cumberland, Chorley, Cheshire West notes for other 2028 cliff readings). Worth flagging into reserves review timing, not raising as a criticism.

IFRS 9 pooled investments and the statutory override
officer.body:
Dear Daniel,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep the data and the training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since a strategy was set. So below are a couple of thoughts on New Forest's Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 approved by Council on 26 February — recognising that under the S101 arrangement much of this sits at your end. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The paper is clearly laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The thing that reads sharpest is the shape of New Forest's debt book. The refinancing indicator in Appendix C at 31 December puts 61% of the PWLB at ten years or longer, and only 5% inside twelve months with another 5% in the following year — 10% inside two years and 23% inside five. Of the councils we have read this year, that is the safe end of the distribution by a distance; refinancing bunches inside three or four years are more common (Medway £245m repricing inside two, Redbridge £108.5m, Northumberland £121m, Shropshire 30% inside two). The book has been built to sit still.

Which frames the second reading. Table 2 in Appendix 1 has internal borrowing rising from £34.5m at 31 March 2025 to £121.7m by 31 March 2029 — an £87m expansion, funded from balance sheet resources drawing down from £66.9m to £35.6m and committed external debt running off from £132.9m to £96.0m before any refinancing decision. Paragraph 1.26 sets the reasoning out plainly: short rates higher than long but expected to fall, so internal or short-term more cost-effective. Six months on, that framing is being validated for reasons the paper couldn't have known. Bank Rate was 3.75% at the point the strategy was set and Arlingclose's Appendix A central case took it to 3.25% by mid-2026; on the 14 August PM fixing it is still 3.75%. And PWLB Certainty rates at the long end have drifted higher rather than lower against the December central case — Arlingclose's Appendix A had the 20-year gilt falling to 4.75% by autumn 2026 (implying c5.55% at the Certainty spread); on the 14 August PM fixing 20-year Certainty is 6.38% and 50-year 6.27%, so the long end sits roughly 80bp above the level the paper's own central case built in. The short-versus-long spread the plan leans on has not narrowed; the value of the internal-and-short-term stance has held up better than the paper's own arithmetic implied.

One smaller observation with a clock on it. Paragraph 1.45 records the pooled-fund unrealised capital loss at £0.336m, sitting against a Treasury Management Reserve balance of £0.300m — a £36k gap. The statutory IFRS 9 override runs to 31 March 2028 for investments made before 1 April 2024, so the reserve has three financial years to absorb any movement before the position reaches the CIES if the underlying doesn't recover. Not a large number, but a dated one.

We price every published council's PWLB book daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, and the liability benchmark pathway sits interactive at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — with CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates it becomes central for everyone, and an interactive version lets you stress the reserves path directly against the shape your Table 3 already prints.

On training, three fit the paper. "Cost of carry and internal borrowing" picks up the £87m decision at the heart of the strategy. "Liability Benchmark: using it in practice" sits directly on Appendix D. "IFRS 9 pooled investments and the statutory override" covers the reserve position with the 2028 clock. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: New Forest District Council Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 Report, Council 26 February 2026, at https://democracy.newforest.gov.uk/documents/s47561/treasury-management-strategy-2026-27-report.pdf
